description: Focused Type-4 positive and hard-negative case handles used by target packets, smoke gates, verifier runs, and regression tests.

hard_negative_groups.claim: Numeric clamp admission must keep bound-order, numeric-domain, shape, and library/API identity hard negatives beside every positive bridge.

Python loop/all plus De Morgan admission must keep vacuous truth, short-circuit timing, helper-call purity, iterator identity, boolean value-context, predicate-coordinate, and effect-safety hard negatives beside the positive packet.

Collection membership admission must keep receiver API/domain proof, searched-element coordinates, collection/source coordinates, and mutation closure beside every literal, factory, imported, or typed dynamic membership bridge.

Collection empty-check admission must keep receiver identity, collection domain/kind, empty-vs-nonempty predicate direction, threshold/cardinality, and mutation closure beside every length-zero or named-empty bridge.

String prefix/suffix admission must keep string receiver identity, affix coordinate identity, API/import identity, prefix-vs-suffix direction, offset overloads, multi-affix disjunctions, and monkey-patched/custom APIs beside every case-sensitive affix bridge.

Null/Option presence and defaulting admission must keep value coordinate, absence channel identity, presence direction, fallback coordinate, nullish-vs-truthy/default timing, and API/channel identity hard negatives beside every nullable or option bridge.

Reduction admission must keep identity/empty behavior, numeric-domain closure for numeric aggregates, step or terminal predicate coordinate, any/all short-circuit direction, selection seed/domain behavior, source identity, receiver/API identity, and effect safety beside every sum/product/any/all/min/max bridge.

Rust Iterator::all admission must keep same-source traversal, vacuous truth, first-counterexample short-circuit direction, pure bool-returning predicates, unconsumed iterator identity, and non-mutating borrow boundaries beside every loop/terminal positive.

cases.claim: Python multi-clause comprehension, nested append loop, and JS flatMap/map compute the same flattened list.
cases.evidence: Focused verify corpus after PR #66: no false merges and complete behavior-equal convergence.

cases.claim: A flattened list is not a nested list of lists.
cases.mutation: FlatMap[A, lambda a. Map[B, lambda b. e]] -> Map[A, lambda a. Map[B, lambda b. e]]
cases.evidence: The #57 equivalence test asserts flat-map and nested-list fingerprints differ.

cases.claim: Mapping to a list without flattening is not one-level flat-map.
cases.mutation: flatMap callback result is kept nested
cases.evidence: Required sibling for any future FlatMap idiom extension.

cases.claim: Literal, factory-backed, imported immutable, and typed dynamic collection membership surfaces can converge when they prove the same searched element and collection receiver/source coordinates.
cases.evidence: The executable replay fixture proves the minimal Python literal membership to JS Set.has bridge and the focused Swift Array.contains bridge; the proof perimeter regression gates cite the broader literal, factory-backed, imported immutable, typed dynamic, and Swift membership suites.

cases.claim: Membership over a different searched element is a different proof coordinate even when the collection receiver is identical.
cases.mutation: contains(value) -> contains(other)
cases.evidence: Literal, typed dynamic, imported, Set/factory, and focused Swift membership tests keep wrong-element fixtures out of the positive membership family.

cases.claim: Membership over different static items, imported providers, or receiver sources changes the collection coordinate.
cases.mutation: ["red", "blue"].contains(value) -> ["green", "blue"].contains(value)
cases.evidence: The membership suites keep wrong-collection literals, factories, imports, package slices, Swift local arrays, and local bindings split.

cases.claim: A contains/has/include-shaped call is not collection membership without a proven receiver domain and API identity.
cases.mutation: collection membership API -> substring contains, JavaScript `in`, raw index/count payload, loose equality, missing import, or shadowed factory
cases.evidence: The focused membership tests reject substring receivers, JavaScript `in`, raw indexOf/findIndex/filter length payloads, loose equality predicates, missing imports, shadowed constructors, Swift custom contains receivers, and untyped dynamic `has` calls.

cases.claim: A collection binding mutated after construction/import no longer proves the original membership predicate.
cases.mutation: construct/import collection -> mutate/add/append/fill/copyWithin/push/insert before membership
cases.evidence: Module, local, provider, importer, and std-factory mutation fixtures across Python, JS/TS, Go, Java, Ruby, Rust, and Swift stay split from the original literal membership family.

cases.claim: Length-zero comparisons and named emptiness predicates converge when they prove the same collection receiver coordinate and empty direction.
cases.evidence: The executable fixture proves the minimal Rust Vec length-zero to is_empty bridge and the Swift Array count == 0 to isEmpty bridge; the proof perimeter regression gates cite broader generated coverage and the Rust/Java/Swift CLI empty-check suite.

cases.claim: Negated named emptiness and nonzero length comparisons converge only as the non-empty direction of the same receiver proof.
cases.evidence: The executable fixture records the non-empty direction separately for Rust and Swift so truthiness/non-emptiness admission cannot be confused with an empty predicate.

cases.claim: A length-one threshold is not strict emptiness, even though it has the same receiver and length surface.
cases.mutation: len(receiver) == 0 -> len(receiver) == 1
cases.evidence: Generated collection_empty_check negatives and the focused Rust/Swift fixtures keep zero-length predicates distinct from one-length/cardinality thresholds.

cases.claim: Emptiness over a different collection parameter is a different receiver coordinate.
cases.mutation: items.is_empty() -> other.is_empty()
cases.evidence: Generated wrong-receiver negatives and the focused Rust/Swift fixtures keep same-shaped emptiness predicates split when the collection coordinate changes.

cases.claim: String and custom isEmpty surfaces are not collection empty-check evidence without compatible receiver domain/kind proof.
cases.mutation: Array.isEmpty -> String.isEmpty or custom isEmpty property
cases.evidence: The Swift focused fixtures keep String.isEmpty and a custom isEmpty property outside Array empty-check admission unless a compatible collection domain/kind proof exists.

cases.claim: A collection mutated before the emptiness predicate no longer proves the original receiver state.
cases.mutation: read receiver emptiness -> mutate receiver, then read emptiness
cases.evidence: The focused Rust/Swift fixtures pin mutation closure so future empty-check expansion cannot treat a stale receiver proof as current state.

cases.claim: Case-sensitive prefix predicates converge across supported receiver/API surfaces when they prove the same string receiver and literal affix coordinate.
cases.evidence: The string_affix_550 CLI fixture proves Python, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, and Swift prefix predicates under exact string receiver, API identity, and literal affix evidence.

cases.claim: Case-sensitive suffix predicates converge when they prove the same string receiver and literal suffix coordinate.
cases.evidence: The string_affix_550 CLI fixture records Python, TypeScript, and Swift suffix direction separately from prefix direction.

cases.claim: Same-role parameter affixes converge across supported languages when the receiver and affix parameter coordinates both match.
cases.evidence: The string_affix_552 coordinate fixture proves TypeScript, Swift, and Python parameter affixes for both prefix and suffix directions when the same parameter role is used.

cases.claim: Direct literal affixes and immutable local/module binding affixes converge when they prove the same affix value coordinate.
cases.evidence: The string_affix_552 coordinate fixture proves immutable Python and Swift literal/local/module binding affixes against direct literal affixes.

cases.claim: Ruby String#start_with? and String#end_with? converge only after literal string receiver proof and standard String API identity are present.
cases.evidence: The Ruby string_affix_551 fixture proves literal string receiver admission for both prefix and suffix directions.

cases.claim: A prefix predicate is not a suffix predicate even when receiver and literal affix coordinates are otherwise compatible.
cases.mutation: prefix predicate -> suffix predicate
cases.evidence: The JS/TS/Python, Swift, and Ruby fixtures keep prefix and suffix directions in separate semantic families.

cases.claim: A string-affix-shaped call without exact string receiver proof, or over a different receiver coordinate, cannot join the proved affix family.
cases.mutation: exact string receiver -> untyped/wrong receiver
cases.evidence: JS/TS receiver hard negatives and wrong-receiver Rust/Swift fixtures remain outside the proved prefix family.

cases.claim: Changing the literal or parameter affix coordinate changes the predicate.
cases.mutation: prefix parameter/literal -> other parameter/literal
cases.evidence: The coordinate fixture keeps wrong TypeScript/Swift parameter roles and changed literal affixes out of proved affix families.

cases.claim: Derived or mutated affix values are not the same coordinate as the original literal or parameter proof.
cases.mutation: literal/parameter affix -> transformed or mutated affix binding
cases.evidence: The coordinate fixture keeps TypeScript/Swift dynamic parameter transformations and mutated prefix/suffix affix bindings outside immutable-coordinate proof.

cases.claim: Offset overloads and tuple/multi-affix disjunctions are not whole-string single-affix predicates until their extra semantics are modeled.
cases.mutation: single whole-string affix -> offset overload or multi-affix disjunction
cases.evidence: JS/Java offset forms may form their own offset family, and Python/Ruby multi-affix forms stay outside the whole-string single-affix proof perimeter.

cases.claim: Ruby same-name custom methods, untyped receivers, wrong receivers, and monkey-patched String APIs do not prove standard String#start_with? identity.
cases.mutation: standard Ruby String affix API -> custom or patched same-name API
cases.evidence: The Ruby fixture keeps custom same-name methods and same-file String monkey patches out of the proved Ruby prefix family.

cases.claim: Swift String.hasPrefix/hasSuffix admission requires the standard case-sensitive String API over the original receiver; substring, custom same-name, and case-normalized variants are not exact affix predicates.
cases.mutation: standard Swift String.hasPrefix -> contains/custom/case-normalized predicate
cases.evidence: The Swift string_affix_550 fixture keeps substring contains, custom same-name hasPrefix methods, and lowercased case-insensitive checks outside the standard case-sensitive String.hasPrefix family.

cases.claim: Null, nil, NULL, and Option absence predicates converge when they prove the same checked value coordinate and absence-channel direction.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports one absence family across C, Go, Java, JS, TS, Python, Ruby nil?, Swift Optional == nil, and Rust Option::is_none/if-let None surfaces.

cases.claim: Non-null and Option present predicates converge separately from absence when they prove the same checked value coordinate and present direction.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports a separate present family across C, Go, Java, JS, TS, Python, Ruby !nil?, Swift Optional != nil, and Rust Option::is_some surfaces.

cases.claim: Nullish/Option defaulting converges when the checked value coordinate and fallback coordinate match and defaulting triggers only on the absence/nullish channel.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports JS `??`, loose-nullish ternary, guard default, TS `??`/ternary, Swift Optional `??`, and Rust Option::unwrap_or in one family; Rust match default remains outside this focused query claim.

cases.claim: Absence and presence predicates are opposite directions and must not merge.
cases.mutation: is absent -> is present
cases.evidence: The focused fixture reports absence and present predicates in separate semantic families, including Ruby nil?/!nil? and Swift == nil/!= nil directions.

cases.claim: Checking a different value coordinate changes the null/Option presence predicate.
cases.mutation: value is None -> other is None
cases.evidence: The focused fixture keeps same-shaped presence tests over `other` out of the `value` presence family, including Ruby nil? and Swift Optional nil comparisons.

cases.claim: Truthy defaulting is not nullish defaulting because falsey present payloads must remain present values.
cases.mutation: value ?? fallback -> value || fallback
cases.evidence: The JS nullish-default CLI tests and focused fixture keep `??`/loose-nullish defaults split from truthiness-based `||` defaults.

cases.claim: Strict-null defaulting is not the same as nullish defaulting because undefined remains a present value under `=== null`.
cases.mutation: value == null ? fallback : value -> value === null ? fallback : value
cases.evidence: The strict-null CLI test records a separate strict-null family and keeps it out of the loose-nullish default family.

cases.claim: Changing the checked value or fallback/default coordinate changes defaulting behavior.
cases.mutation: value ?? fallback -> other ?? fallback or value ?? otherDefault
cases.evidence: Focused defaulting and option-boundary equivalence tests keep wrong-value and wrong-fallback coordinates split from the proved default family, including Swift Optional `??`.

cases.claim: Ruby nil? and Swift nil comparisons must require standard API/channel identity and the original checked coordinate.
cases.mutation: standard nil?/Optional == nil over value -> redefined nil?, custom nil-literal equality, or rebound checked value
cases.evidence: The focused fixture and option-boundaries equivalence tests keep Ruby same-file class/singleton/top-level nil? methods, literal, dynamic, send/public_send, immediate Method#call, and stored Method#call define_method/define_singleton_method nil? changes, literal and dynamic nil? alias/undef changes, Swift custom nil-literal/equality overloads including Optional-typed overloads, and rebound checked values outside the standard absence family.

cases.claim: Swift nil-coalescing admission must require Optional API identity and an already-evaluated fallback coordinate.
cases.mutation: Optional value ?? fallback -> custom ?? overload or value ?? expensive()
cases.evidence: The focused fixture and option-boundaries equivalence tests admit Swift `??` only for Optional-typed checked values with literal, variable, or parameter fallbacks; effectful call fallbacks, computed property fallbacks, and custom overload domains including Optional-typed overloads stay split.

cases.claim: Result Ok/Err channels are not Option Some/None channels even when predicate names and defaulting APIs look similar.
cases.mutation: Option Some/None channel -> Result Ok/Err channel
cases.evidence: The Rust option-boundaries equivalence suite keeps Option Some/None predicates distinct from Result Ok/Err predicates and keeps Result defaulting APIs outside the narrow Option/nullish default slice.

cases.claim: filter_map-style option-producing callbacks can converge with explicit filter+map where None drops elements.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test and hof_filter_map smoke converge Python filtered comprehension, JS filter().map(), Rust filter_map Some/None, and Rust guarded Vec::new()/push builder.

cases.claim: Dropping None differs from mapping None as a value.
cases.mutation: filter_map callback returns None where map keeps a sentinel value
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test rejects a Rust map that emits Option payloads instead of dropping None.

cases.claim: Changing the mapped Some value changes behavior even when the predicate stays the same.
cases.mutation: Some(x) -> Some(x + 1)
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test rejects Some(x * 3) against the covered Some(x * 2) value coordinate.

cases.claim: filter_map keeps falsey Some-like values; only Null/None absence drops an item.
cases.mutation: coerce the callback result through truthiness before deciding whether to emit it
cases.evidence: Interpreter FilterMap tests keep Int(0), and focused equivalence test converges Some(0) with a filtered zero map while rejecting a later truthy zero filter.

cases.claim: Richer option-producing match/and_then forms may converge with explicit filter+map when they preserve the same absence and emitted-value coordinates.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test and hof_filter_map smoke converge Python/TypeScript filter+map with Rust match-guard and pure Option::and_then filter_map callbacks.

cases.claim: A wrapped None payload is an emitted value in richer option domains, not the current Null absence sentinel.
cases.mutation: Some(None)-style payload vs None absence
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test converges Rust Some(None) payloads with Python filtered None values and rejects them against mapped x*2 values.

cases.claim: A sum over a flat-map stream equals the corresponding nested reduction loop.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test converges Python sum over a flat-map generator, Python nested reduction loop, and JS flatMap().reduce().

cases.claim: A zero-seeded nested selection loop clamps at its seed (returns 0 on empty or all-negative input); true max over the flat-map stream does not.
cases.evidence: nose verify flagged the previous positive labeling as a false merge (10 differing inputs) once 2-argument min/max became interpretable; selection reductions now key their seed, and the focused equivalence test asserts the fingerprints differ while equal-seeded loops still converge.

cases.claim: An any/existence reduction over a flat-map stream equals the corresponding nested early-return loop.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test converges any(x + y > 0 for x in xs for y in ys) with a nested early-return existence loop.

cases.claim: Changing the reduction seed changes aggregate behavior.
cases.mutation: sum seed 0 -> 1
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test keeps a nested sum loop seeded with 1 distinct from the flat-map sum seeded with 0.

cases.claim: Aggregating a nested list shape differs from aggregating a flattened stream unless a separate flatten is proven.
cases.mutation: flat stream -> nested list
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test keeps sum over nested list rows distinct from sum over the flattened stream.

cases.claim: Changing the flattened any predicate changes behavior.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test keeps the inverted predicate distinct from the covered > predicate.

cases.claim: A flat-map aggregate whose emitted value ignores the outer element still depends on the outer collection cardinality.
cases.mutation: sum(y for x in xs for y in ys) -> sum(y for y in ys)
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test keeps the outer-ignored flat-map aggregate and nested loop distinct from the direct inner sum.

cases.claim: A filtered flat-map aggregate may converge with an equivalent nested guarded reduction when outer and inner predicates are preserved.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test converges Python filtered flat-map sum, Python nested guarded sum loop, JS filtered flatMap().reduce(), and JS method-terminal .some()/.every() with the equivalent Python filtered any/all generators.

cases.claim: Changing an outer or inner FlatMap aggregate predicate changes behavior.
cases.mutation: outer/inner/terminal predicate changed to a static false predicate while contribution stays the same
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test keeps static-false outer predicates, inner predicates, and method-terminal predicates distinct from the covered filtered FlatMap aggregate.

cases.claim: A filtered FlatMap any/all existence or universal aggregate may converge with the equivalent nested guarded early-return loop.
cases.evidence: Focused equivalence test converges Python filtered any/all generators, JS filtered flatMap().some()/every(), and equivalent Python nested guarded early-return loops.

cases.claim: Sum loops, typed reduce/fold terminals, and standard sum APIs can converge in the focused integer/value-model numeric domain when source, identity, empty behavior, and additive step coordinates match.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports one semantic family spanning C for/while, Go range/index, Java loop/reduce, JS loop, Python loop/sum, Rust loop/sum, and typed TypeScript loop/reduce surfaces under the detector's focused integer/value-model numeric abstraction.

cases.claim: Changing the explicit reduction seed changes empty-input behavior and non-empty aggregate results.
cases.mutation: sum seed 0 -> 1
cases.evidence: The focused fixture keeps the seed-1 Python and TypeScript reductions outside the seed-0 sum family.

cases.claim: Changing the reduction step or contribution expression changes behavior even when traversal is identical.
cases.mutation: additive step -> multiplicative step or counted contribution
cases.evidence: The focused fixture keeps additive sums, products, and positive-count reductions in distinct semantic families.

cases.claim: Any/all terminal predicates can converge with equivalent early-return loops when source, predicate, empty result, and short-circuit direction match.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports TypeScript any/some, Rust any/Iterator::any, and Rust all/Iterator::all loop-terminal families with separate changed-predicate and changed-direction siblings.

cases.claim: Changing the any/all terminal predicate or short-circuit direction changes behavior.
cases.evidence: The Rust and TypeScript terminal fixtures keep changed predicates out of the admitted any/all families, and the Rust terminal fixture keeps any(x > 0) separate from all(x > 0).

cases.claim: A TypeScript Array.every(...) universal predicate can converge with a same-source for-of counterexample loop when dense literal source evidence closes sparse-hole behavior, the callback observes only the element value, the loop returns false on the first failing boolean predicate, and true after exhaustion.
cases.evidence: The TypeScript fixture admits only the dense-literal Array.every surface whose for-of loop traverses the same parameterized literal source [a, b, c], returns false on the first counterexample against min, preserves vacuous truth, and uses a one-argument comparison predicate whose result is boolean even when JS/TS relational coercion keeps the comparison value opaque.

cases.claim: A TypeScript number[] parameter is not dense-source proof for Array.every(...) because sparse array holes are skipped by every but can be observed by for-of iteration.
cases.mutation: dense literal source evidence -> plain number[] parameter
cases.evidence: For a sparse runtime array such as new Array(1), Array.every skips the hole and returns true while the for-of loop can visit undefined and reject the comparison; a TypeScript number[] annotation alone does not rule that out.

cases.claim: Changing the for-of loop fallthrough result breaks Array.every(...) vacuous truth.
cases.mutation: fallthrough return true -> false
cases.evidence: tsAllWrongEmptyTruth returns false for empty input while Array.every(...) returns true.

cases.claim: Changing the Array.every(...) predicate changes behavior even when the surface remains universal.
cases.evidence: tsAllChangedPredicate uses a strict threshold coordinate, so values equal to min are accepted by tsAllEvery and rejected by the changed predicate.

cases.claim: The Array.every(...) receiver and for-of loop source must be the same collection.
cases.mutation: loop traverses ys while every traverses xs
cases.evidence: tsAllDifferentSource has the same predicate and vacuous-truth shape but iterates [a, b, d] while tsAllEvery traverses [a, b, c], so source-coordinate identity is behavior-defining without relying on an always-false literal.

cases.claim: Callback or loop-body effects prevent treating Array.every(...) and a counterexample loop as a pure boolean rewrite.
cases.mutation: insert observed seen.push(x) in the callback or counterexample branch
cases.evidence: Both hard negatives keep the same `(seen, bad, ok)` signature; only the callback or the failing loop branch can observe a push effect.

cases.claim: Array.every(...) callbacks that observe the index or source-array arguments stay outside the value-only universal predicate proof.
cases.mutation: one-argument element predicate -> callback observes index or source array
cases.evidence: tsEveryIndexLong can fail solely because the third index is observable, and tsEverySourceArrayLong can fail solely because the callback source array has length 3; the admitted value-only proof binds only the element coordinate.

cases.claim: JS/TS value-returning && operands are not boolean-only predicate evidence.
cases.mutation: proven comparison predicate conjunction -> value-returning x && comparison
cases.evidence: tsEveryValueReturningAnd uses `x && ...`, whose left operand is a value/truthiness payload rather than a proven boolean comparison result.

cases.claim: A JavaScript Array.every(...) universal predicate can converge with a same-source for-of counterexample loop when dense literal source evidence closes sparse-hole behavior, the callback observes only the element value, the loop returns false on the first failing boolean predicate, and true after exhaustion.
cases.evidence: The JavaScript fixture admits only the dense-literal Array.every surface whose for-of loop traverses the same parameterized literal source [a, b, c], returns false on the first counterexample against min, preserves vacuous truth, and uses a one-argument comparison predicate; arbitrary JavaScript array parameters remain outside the dense-source proof.

cases.claim: A JavaScript array parameter is not dense-source proof for Array.every(...) because sparse array holes are skipped by every but can be observed by for-of iteration.
cases.mutation: dense literal source evidence -> plain array parameter
cases.evidence: For a sparse runtime array such as new Array(1), Array.every skips the hole and returns true while the for-of loop can visit undefined and reject the comparison; an unproven JavaScript array parameter does not rule that out.

cases.claim: Changing the for-of loop fallthrough result breaks JavaScript Array.every(...) vacuous truth.
cases.mutation: fallthrough return true -> false
cases.evidence: jsAllWrongEmptyTruth returns false for empty input while Array.every(...) returns true.

cases.claim: Changing the JavaScript Array.every(...) predicate changes behavior even when the surface remains universal.
cases.mutation: x >= min -> x > min
cases.evidence: jsAllChangedPredicate uses a strict threshold coordinate, so values equal to min are accepted by jsAllEvery and rejected by the changed predicate.

cases.claim: The JavaScript Array.every(...) receiver and for-of loop source must be the same collection.
cases.mutation: loop traverses ys while every traverses xs
cases.evidence: jsAllDifferentSource has the same predicate and vacuous-truth shape but iterates [a, b, d] while jsAllEvery traverses [a, b, c], so source-coordinate identity is behavior-defining.

cases.claim: Callback or loop-body effects prevent treating JavaScript Array.every(...) and a counterexample loop as a pure boolean rewrite.
cases.mutation: insert observed seen.push(x) in the callback or counterexample branch
cases.evidence: Both hard negatives keep the same `(seen, bad, ok)` signature; only the callback or the failing loop branch can observe a push effect.

cases.claim: JavaScript Array.every(...) callbacks that observe the index or source-array arguments stay outside the value-only universal predicate proof.
cases.mutation: one-argument element predicate -> callback observes index or source array
cases.evidence: jsEveryIndexLong can fail solely because the third index is observable, and jsEverySourceArrayLong can fail solely because the callback source array has length 3; the admitted value-only proof binds only the element coordinate.

cases.claim: JavaScript value-returning && operands are not boolean-only predicate evidence.
cases.mutation: proven comparison predicate conjunction -> value-returning x && comparison
cases.evidence: jsEveryValueReturningAnd uses `x && ...`, whose left operand is a value/truthiness payload rather than a proven boolean comparison result.

cases.claim: JavaScript Array.every(...) admission requires standard Array.prototype.every API identity in the same file.
cases.mutation: standard Array.prototype.every -> same-file prototype replacement
cases.evidence: Same-file Array.prototype.every assignment and Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, "every", ...) can replace the standard terminal API, so the loop/every proof must stay closed when those writes are present.

cases.claim: A Rust Iterator::all(...) terminal can converge with a same-source counterexample loop when the receiver is proven as the same iterator source, the predicate is pure and bool-returning, the loop returns false at the first failing predicate, and both forms preserve vacuous truth.
cases.evidence: The Rust fixture admits the standard `xs.iter().copied().all(|x| x >= 0)` surface and its empty-source sibling only when the loop scans the same source and falls through to true after exhaustion.

cases.claim: Changing the loop fallthrough result breaks Rust Iterator::all(...) vacuous truth.
cases.mutation: fallthrough return true -> false
cases.evidence: rust_all_wrong_empty_truth returns false for empty input while Iterator::all(...) returns true.

cases.claim: Changing the Rust Iterator::all(...) predicate changes behavior even when the surface remains universal.
cases.evidence: rust_all_positive_iter rejects zero while rust_all_iter accepts it, so predicate-coordinate identity is required independently from the universal surface spelling.

cases.claim: The Rust Iterator::all(...) receiver and counterexample loop source must be the same collection or iterator source.
cases.mutation: terminal traverses ys while the positive source traverses xs
cases.evidence: Both functions keep the same `(xs, ys)` surface, but one terminal traverses xs and the other traverses ys.

cases.claim: Closure or loop-body effects prevent treating Rust Iterator::all(...) and a counterexample loop as a pure boolean rewrite.
cases.mutation: insert observed log.push(x) in the callback or failing loop branch
cases.evidence: All three functions expose the same `log` parameter; only the callback or failing loop branch mutates it.

cases.claim: A Rust iterator that has already been advanced is not the same full-source traversal as the counterexample loop.
cases.mutation: fresh xs.iter().copied() -> iter.next(); iter.all(...)
cases.evidence: rust_all_consumed_iterator skips the first element before calling all, so iterator identity must include consumption state rather than just the source name.

cases.claim: Rust Iterator::all(...) over iter_mut with writes through borrowed elements is behavior-defining and must stay outside the pure predicate perimeter.
cases.mutation: iter().copied() pure predicate -> iter_mut() predicate that writes *x
cases.evidence: rust_all_mutating_borrow changes the borrowed slice through `*x += 1`; the Rust terminal callback admission now requires the callback body to be effect-closed before it can normalize to a pure all reduction.

cases.claim: Rust has no JS/TS-style value-returning Iterator::all predicate surface: the standard callback type is bool-returning, so value-payload truthiness is closed at the type boundary.
cases.mutation: bool-returning predicate -> non-bool value-returning predicate
cases.evidence: No valid executable Rust Iterator::all pair exists for this boundary because `Iterator::all` requires `FnMut(Self::Item) -> bool`; the executable siblings above cover the remaining behavior-defining predicate-coordinate and effect boundaries.

cases.claim: Seeded min/max selection loops and folds can converge when they preserve the same seed, comparator direction, and selection domain.
cases.evidence: The focused executable fixture reports separate seeded max and seeded min families across Python loops/reduce and Rust loops/folds.

cases.claim: Selection reductions must preserve comparator direction, explicit seed, and empty/all-negative behavior; unseeded terminal APIs are not the same as clamped seeded loops.
cases.mutation: max selection -> min selection; seeded max loop -> unseeded max().unwrap_or(0)
cases.evidence: The focused fixture keeps max and min selection directions separate and keeps unseeded max().unwrap_or(0) outside the seeded max family because all-negative non-empty inputs differ.

cases.claim: Ruby Enumerable quantifier admission must stay closed for unproven receiver parameters, changed predicates or sources, observable block effects, multi-parameter block destructuring, no-block Enumerable semantics, and same-file Array/Enumerable monkey patches.
cases.mutation: proven literal Array receiver and pure single-value block -> unproven/custom receiver, changed predicate/source, effectful/multi-parameter/no block, or patched Enumerable API
cases.evidence: The focused Ruby fixture keeps receiver parameters, changed predicate/source coordinates, observed block effects, multi-parameter block destructuring, no-block semantics, and same-file Array#any? or Enumerable.module_eval redefinitions outside the proved Ruby Enumerable quantifier family.

cases.claim: Ruby Enumerable any?/all? over a proven literal Array receiver can converge with equivalent early-return loops when the source, predicate, empty result, short-circuit direction, receiver API identity, and block effect boundary match.
cases.evidence: The focused Ruby fixture admits only literal Array receiver any?/all? blocks with pure one-argument predicates, matching early-return loop direction, and all? vacuous truth over an empty literal Array.

cases.claim: Swift allSatisfy admission must stay closed for changed predicates or sources, changed empty-input truth, observable callback or loop effects, lazy receiver demand semantics, and custom overloads with non-value-only callback shape.
cases.mutation: proven Array/Collection receiver and pure inline allSatisfy predicate -> changed predicate/source, wrong fallthrough, effectful predicate/loop, lazy adapter receiver, or two-argument overload callback
cases.evidence: The focused Swift fixture keeps changed predicate/source coordinates, wrong vacuous truth, observed callback or loop effects, .lazy allSatisfy demand semantics, and a typechecked two-argument custom overload outside the proved eager Array/Collection allSatisfy family.

cases.claim: Swift allSatisfy over a proven Array/Collection receiver can converge with an equivalent counterexample loop when source identity, terminal predicate coordinate, universal short-circuit direction, vacuous truth, eager receiver demand, and predicate purity match.
cases.evidence: The focused Swift fixture admits eager Array/Collection allSatisfy only for pure inline one-argument predicates over the same receiver/source, including empty-input vacuous truth.

cases.claim: A pure Java Stream.flatMap chain can express the same one-level flat-map as Python multi-clause comprehension.
